<description>
{
 "summary": "Replaces the FreeBSD cross-compilation CI job with a native build and test suite run inside a FreeBSD virtual machine using vmactions/freebsd-vm. Adapts CI environment scripts for FreeBSD native tooling, silences lockf warnings from FreeBSD lsof in the test runner, and integrates a custom HTTPConnection in functional tests to avoid BSD ephemeral port collisions.",
 "problem": "FreeBSD binaries are only cross-compiled in pull request CI without running unit or functional tests, allowing platform-specific regressions to reach the main branch until detected in nightly builds. Running tests natively on FreeBSD also triggers functional test failures due to ephemeral port collisions and lsof lockf warnings on stderr.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"We currently cross-compile BSD binaries without testing them in this repository. Running tests before merge should help catch platform-specific regressions that would otherwise first appear in nightly builds.\"",
  "Commit a2c3b1e27f: \"FreeBSD and OpenBSD allocate ephemeral ports from ranges that overlap the functional framework's fixed test ports. An outgoing localhost connection can therefore select its destination port as its source port and connect to itself. The wrong-RPC-port startup test exposed this on FreeBSD as BadStatusLine: POST / HTTP/1.1\"",
  "Commit e29fe9068c: \"FreeBSD lsof can emit the following warning during parallel tests: lsof: WARNING -- reading lockf list failed: Cannot allocate memory. The functional test runner treats nonempty stderr as failure even when a test exits successfully.\""
 ],

 },

<category name="build" title="Build and CI">
## Covers

How the project is built, tested, and released: the CMake build system,
the depends system and its packages, Guix reproducible builds, CI
configuration and scripts, compiler and platform support, and the
tooling under contrib used for releases and development. Platform
labels (Windows, macOS) point here when the change is about building or
running on that platform rather than about a feature. The Build system
label is a strong prior.

Not build: source changes that happen to fix a compiler warning as a
side effect (they belong to their area).

## What matters here

Release integrity first: reproducibility of Guix builds, correctness of
dependency pinning and verification, and anything that could ship a
wrong binary. Then supported-platform breakage: a platform that fails
to build or run blocks users on it. Then CI reliability: flaky or
misleading jobs waste every contributor's time and hide real failures.
Then dependency transitions with deadlines (compiler or library minimum
versions, deprecations upstream). Then build time and contributor
friction.

Cosmetic CMake cleanups rank low unless they remove a recurring
breakage.

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.

<category name="tests" title="Test infrastructure">
## Covers

The machinery of testing rather than tests of a particular area: the
functional test framework and runner, unit test utilities, the fuzzing
harnesses and corpora, benchmarks, linters, sanitizer configuration,
and fixes for flaky tests whose cause is in the framework. A test that
pins the behavior of one area (a wallet migration test, a p2p relay
test) belongs to that area, not here. The Tests and Fuzzing labels are
a prior, but a labeled PR whose tests are about one area goes to that
area instead.

## What matters here

Signal first: fixes for flaky or misleading tests, since a red CI that
nobody trusts hides real failures. Then coverage of high-risk code paths
that the fuzzers or functional tests do not reach, especially
consensus, mempool policy, and p2p message handling. Then framework
capabilities that unblock tests other areas need. Then test speed, which
every contributor pays for on every run. Then cleanliness of the test
code.

Adding tests for their own sake ranks low; adding a test that catches a
realistic regression ranks high.
